full_judgment: 12. In a case before the Federal Court (A.I.R. 1943 (F.C), 24) a suit was instituted in 1932 in British India with respect to properties situated in British India and also in Burma, it was held that the suit could be continued in British India with respect to properties in Burma even after Burma had been separated in 1937. The principle enunciated seems to be that a right to continue a duly instituted suit is in the nature of a vested right and it cannot be taken away except by a clear indication of intention to that affect. In the absence of such a clear indication in the Constitution Act, a British Indian Court had jurisdiction to continue with trial of a suit already pending before it even with respect to properties situated in Burma. In the other case reported in A.I.R. 1950 (Hyderabad) 71 the facts are that by section 2 of India and Hyderabad Exchanges of Enclaves Order, 1950, the Hyderabad enclaves in Bombay were included and made part of the Province of Bombay and under section 2(e) of the Order read with Article 2(a) of the Agreement between the Governor General of India and the Nizam of Hyderabad dated 23-1-1950, the transfer of the enclaves became effective on 25-1-1950, i.e. before the Constitution of India came into force. It was held that in the absence of clear intention to the contrary the transfer of the territory did not affect the vested jurisdiction of the Magistrate in the territory transferred in a case pending before him at the time of the transfer and he continues to exercise the same even after the transfer of the territory. The principles enunciated in these two cases and applied in far more radical facts than that of the present case, in my opinion, support the proposition, at least, that the District Judge, Comilla did not lose his jurisdiction to pronounce judgment in the matter on 22-9-84 notwithstanding the fact that the territorial jurisdiction vested with the District Judge, Chandpur on and from 1-9-84.
